extracted.intended_audience: general readers of ethical/philosophical essays; educated readers interested in practical moral reflection
extracted.subtask_description: An early-modern personal/philosophical essay reflecting on how to live and die, valuing naturalness, simplicity, and practical judgment over artifice and over-anticipation. The text offers normative maxims about conduct, teaching, death, beauty, trust, and the use of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: That we cannot fail in following Nature / conform to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “That we cannot fail in following Nature,” — the sovereign precept is to conform ourselves to nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne repeatedly asserts that the chief rule of life is to follow natural inclinations rather than overcorrect them with art. He treats natural disposition as the primary guide for conduct and as more reliable than artificial precepts. Example/contrast: Socrates corrected his natural composition by reason, but Montaigne prefers to let his own nature remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-anticipate or meditate upon evils (avoid preparing yourself into misery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipating future misfortunes (banishments, tortures, wars, diseases, shipwrecks) troubles us as much as suffering; 'It troubles men as much that they may possibly suffer, as if they really did suffer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imagining and rehearsing extreme evils in advance; such premeditation often does more harm than the actual event. The recommended practice is to banish anxious thoughts of possible evils because 'we shall find them heavy enough when they come.' Anti-pattern: rehearsing worst-case disasters and thereby making oneself miserable now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust nature to teach you how to die
rubrics_metrics.description: If you do not know how to die, do not trouble yourself; 'nature will, at the time, fully and sufficiently instruct you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation for death that consists in constant premeditation is unnecessary and often harmful — sudden or unpremeditated death can be less painful than long fear. Philosophy may advise meditating on death, but it should give rules so that foresight does not harm; otherwise, rely on natural courage and the present moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simplicity and truth over rhetorical embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates' simple, plain pleading at his trial is held up as superior to an ornate, premeditated oratorical defence; 'not to corrupt the tenor of an incorrupt life... to adorn and deck herself with the embellishments of figures' would be unworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In speech and conduct, truth and natural simplicity are more admirable than polished artifice. Example: Socrates spoke simply and honestly rather than using a courtly, rhetorical speech; Montaigne praises that 'inartificial boldness and infantine security.' Anti-pattern: exchanging genuine character for ornamented performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value invention (original thought) over mere allegation/compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'a great and incomparable preference in the honour of invention over that of allegation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assembling borrowed commonplaces or compiling others' material is inferior to producing original thought. Montaigne criticizes writers who compile without understanding and those who buy or borrow books rather than make one. Anti-patterns: creating works composed mainly of unexamined quotations or delegated compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor instruction and consolation to people's capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Men differ in sentiment and force; we must lead them to their own good according to their capacities and by various ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral teaching and consolation should not be one-size-fits-all; adapt methods to individual temperament and ability. Example: simplicity may be as effective as learned lessons for many; different people need different approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let the fear of future harm rob you of present life
rubrics_metrics.description: It is folly 'to lose the present for fear of the future' or 'to make thyself miserable now, because thou art to be so in time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize present enjoyment and steadiness of life over ruinous anticipation. Philosophy should give precautions so that thought of the future doesn't destroy present well-being; otherwise, favour living fully now.

rubrics_metrics.name: A person's look is but a feeble warranty — use physiognomy cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's look can give an impression but is only a weak guarantee of character: 'A person’s look is but a feeble warranty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearances often influence judgment (beauty seduces and prepossesses), and some faces seem 'lucky' or 'unlucky,' but physiognomy is unreliable. While Montaigne admits some art in distinguishing temperaments by features, he warns against overreliance; treat appearance as suggestive rather than determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and use the social power of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty has priority in social dealings: it 'presents itself in the front; seduces and prepossesses our judgments with great authority and wonderful impression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that beauty yields practical advantages (influence, trust, leniency). Historical examples: Phryne, Cyrus, Alexander, Caesar. Guidance is descriptive — acknowledge beauty's effect and don't ignore it when judging or acting in social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish superficial ugliness from substantial deformity when judging character
rubrics_metrics.description: Superficial or sudden unseemliness at first sight (a spot, rugged countenance) often disgusts but is less prejudicial to the mind than deeper, substantial deformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate first impressions of ugliness with moral defect; some people with unattractive faces may possess probity and trustworthiness. Conversely, beauty can mask malignity. Use care and discernment rather than a crude aesthetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default to trust and excuse rather than suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne describes himself as 'very little inclined to suspicion' and willing to 'incline towards excuse and the gentlest interpretation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume ordinary human behavior unless clear evidence suggests otherwise; this disposition can avert conflict and sometimes avert dangers (examples where his frankness defused treachery). Anti-pattern: excessive distrust that shortens one's reach and ability to act freely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mercy and prevention over harsh punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging criminals, Montaigne claims he has 'rather chosen to fail in point of justice than to do it' and quotes 'I had rather men should not commit faults than that I should have sufficient courage to condemn them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor measures that prevent wrongdoing and preserve people rather than punitive severity. Mercy to persons need not mean toleration of wrongdoing itself (Aristotle: 'merciful to the man, but not to his wickedness'); but overall, err on the side of leniency where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/devotional belief alone is insufficient without conduct (distinguish devotion from conscience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use demonstrates a distinction between devotion and conscience; belief without proper conduct is 'ruinous to all government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake mere profession of religion for moral behavior; civic order and ethical action require more than ritual or asserted beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid producing works that are merely collections of unread/ununderstood commonplaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Books 'made of things that were never either studied or understood' or composed mainly by delegating examination to learned friends are criticized as buying or borrowing a book rather than making one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writing or scholarship, prefer engaging understanding and original composition over assembling quotations and secondhand material. Anti-pattern: delegating investigation and offering only ink and paper as one's contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the limits of foresight; do not ascribe excessive control to human prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne counsels that we 'pretend to more from our own conduct than appertains to us' and that Heaven cuts short designs to remind us of our limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the role of fortune/divine will in outcomes; avoid overplanning and the illusion that careful prudence can fully control events. Practical effect: be prepared to rely on luck and on others; humility about one's agency is advised.
